# Part I. Full English Translation of the Japanese Canonical Original

## One-sentence definition

> **A language base in Information Engineering is a foundational representational system for preserving, operating on, and reusing information generated through cognition as efficiently as possible while losing as little as possible of meaning, relations, context, state, and uncertainty. For this purpose, this paper adopts Japanese as the base language.**

---

# 0. Theory state of this paper

This paper begins from the current structural understanding:

```text
world
↓
cognition
↓
information
↓
information operation
```

But this sequence is not declared to be the final hierarchy of the pre-cognitive world-itself.

When this paper says that “information is a product of cognition,” that claim is strongly adopted under the current definition of v0.4. At the same time, if future observations require reconstructing the distinctions among cognition, information, subject, target, and external world themselves, the definition of information is reopened from upstream.

Likewise, using Japanese as the base language is not a declaration that “Japanese will eternally be the strongest language.”

> **It is a strong within-version design decision to adopt Japanese as the base language for the current targets, purposes, and requirements for preserving semantic structure.**

When reopened, the audit does not merely swap languages. It returns upstream to:

- what counts as information,
- what counts as loss,
- what counts as preservation of semantic structure,
- which cognitive subject, use case, and time axis are being targeted,
- and which comparison axes were used.

“Provisional” does not mean arbitrarily changeable. Under current conditions, Japanese as the base language is fixed as a rule. A change requires concrete observations, implementation results, or structural changes that break the current judgment.

---

## Abstract

Information is not an object that simply exists in the world as information.

Even if differences or interactions exist in the world, for them to become “information” requires detection, targeting, differentiation, relation-building, meaning assignment, and related operations by a cognitive subject.

Therefore:

> **Information is a product of cognition.**

The current basic relation adopted in this paper is:

```text
world
↓
cognition
↓
information
↓
operation of information
```

From this structure, under the current definition of v0.4, this paper does not adopt “Information Science” as an independent Science. Information is a cognition-after product established downstream of cognition, and recording, encoding, storage, transmission, retrieval, transformation, combination, computation, and reuse are purpose-bound problems of operating on and designing with information. This paper therefore treats that activity as **Information Engineering**.

The performance of Information Engineering is not determined only by bit count, communication speed, compression ratio, or computation speed. It also matters how much of the meaning, relations, context, differences, and uncertainty established through cognition can be carried into subsequent processing without being destroyed. This paper calls that property **semantic-structure preservation efficiency**.

The principal information-operation infrastructure that humanity has used for long periods for this purpose is language. Language is not merely a means of conversation. It is an Information Engineering infrastructure that externalizes cognitive results, names targets, preserves differences, describes relations, preserves them across time, and re-inputs them into the cognition of others and later generations.

This paper evaluates the structure of Japanese for this purpose. Japanese can use kanji, kana, particles, inflection, sentence endings, omission, and context on the same representational surface, allowing meaning, relations, stance, shared state, and uncertainty to be retained in multiple layers. This characteristic has high suitability for the theory generation, structuring, auditing, and reuse demanded by this theoretical system.

Therefore, in this theoretical system:

> **Japanese is the sole base and normative language. The Japanese original is established first, and translation into other languages is performed only downstream when operationally necessary.**

---

# 1. What is information?

Even if light, sound, objects, and change exist in the world, this paper does not call them “information” merely because they exist.

When a cognitive subject detects something, distinguishes it from something else, carves it out as a target, recognizes its state, relates it to other targets, and assigns meaning to it, that difference becomes information the subject can handle.

Accordingly, this paper defines information as:

> **That which has been carved out from the world through cognition and converted into a state operable by a subject.**

This is a within-version definition of v0.4. The terms “subject,” “world,” “cognition,” “meaning,” and “operable” are not fixed entities either. If new observations change those distinctions, the definition of information itself is reconstructed.

---

# 2. Why “Information Science” does not hold

As separated in the preceding paper, “What Is Cognitive Engineering?”, Science is the activity of observing what holds in observable phenomena, actions, and relations, whereas Engineering sets a purpose, acts on a target, and realizes an intended state.

Information is a downstream target established through cognition.

The principal activities generally conducted under the name “information” include encoding, recording, storage, compression, transmission, retrieval, classification, transformation, computation, combination, inference, and reuse.

These are questions of:

> **how to handle information.**

They are operation and design problems.

Therefore:

> **Under the current definition of v0.4, this paper does not recognize an independent Science called “Information Science.”**

> **Establishment judgment lock: Information Science does not hold.**

What is denied here is not the social existence of the name “Information Science,” academic societies, research activity, or institutions. What this paper denies is its establishment **as an independent Science whose target is information itself after that information has been established through cognition**.

The institutional existence of a name is not a refutation of this establishment judgment. Refutation or reopening requires observation or argument that breaks the establishment relation “world → cognition → information,” the definition of information, or the Science/Engineering separation adopted by this paper.

This claim must not be weakened into “mere reclassification” or “a terminological preference.”

This paper does not deny individual useful research or technologies conducted under the existing label “Information Science.” What it denies is the classification.

The activity of handling information generated through cognition according to a purpose is, in principle, **Information Engineering**.

This judgment remains auditable, but it is not weakened by unsupported possibility reservations. Reopening requires a concrete re-separation that changes where information is established or changes the establishment conditions of Science and Engineering.

---

# 3. Difference from the critique of Cognitive Science

The critique of Cognitive Science and the critique of Information Science are not the same.

The problem with Cognitive Science is:

> **Can cognition itself, which cannot be directly observed, be treated as an object of Science through a model constructed from cognition-after external phenomena?**

The problem with Information Science lies further downstream:

> **Why should information generated by that cognition constitute an independent object of Science?**

```text
world
↓
cognition       ← establishment problem of Cognitive Science
↓
information     ← establishment problem of Information Science
↓
information operation ← Information Engineering
```

This diagram itself is a current explanatory Projection. The important point is not to confuse the positions at which the two criticisms arise.

---

# 4. What does Information Engineering do?

The purpose of Information Engineering is not to explain information as an independent ontological entity.

It is:

> **To handle information established through cognition, according to purpose, with little loss and with high efficiency.**

Performance therefore includes more than raw processing speed:

- Is the necessary meaning preserved?
- Are relations among targets preserved?
- Is context preserved?
- Are original differences collapsed?
- Is uncertainty turned into certainty without justification?
- Can the information later be reinterpreted?
- Can it be reused for another purpose?

This paper groups these properties under the term:

> **semantic-structure preservation efficiency.**

However, “meaning,” “structure,” “preservation,” and “efficiency” themselves may change with use case, subject, time, or implementation. The comparison axes themselves are therefore not exempt from future audit.

---

# 5. Information quantity and semantic-structure preservation efficiency are different

Bit count, compression ratio, communication speed, and computation speed matter. But they are not sufficient to evaluate how efficiently information generated through cognition is handled.

A huge concept may be referenced by an extremely short symbol, but if the concept cannot be reconstructed, this does not amount to successful semantic processing.

Conversely, if everything is expanded in full prose every time, explicitness increases, but operation efficiency is low if enormous re-expansion is always required.

What matters is therefore:

> **Preserving the required semantic structure even while compressed, and being able to re-expand it when necessary.**

“Efficiency” in this paper does not refer only to the quantity of information on a communication channel.

---

# 6. Language is an information-operation infrastructure

Language is not merely a means of conversation.

Language externalizes cognitive results, gives names to targets, preserves differences, describes relations, shares states, preserves past cognition into the future, inputs it into the cognition of others, combines multiple pieces of information, and generates new cognition.

Therefore:

> **Language is a vast Information Engineering infrastructure constructed by humanity.**

Civilization-scale information inheritance requires not only oral operation but recorded operation.

Spoken language before writing cannot be directly observed today. It is a natural inference that spoken language existed before writing, but that is not an observed fact in the sense that pre-writing speech itself can be directly accessed now. This paper preserves that distinction.

---

# 7. Structure of Japanese

This paper does not treat Japanese as a simple, single-line phonetic language.

Modern Japanese overlays multiple lineages: oral lineages centered on native Japanese language, lineages of semantic description and conceptual recording introduced through kanji and Classical Chinese, kana for recording Japanese sound and grammar, and the combined operation of Sino-Japanese, native Japanese, and loan vocabulary.

It is not the purpose of this paper to fix every historical origin uniquely.

What matters is the structure observable now.

> **Japanese can use, within the same sentence, symbols that strongly preserve semantic distinctions together with symbols that describe sound, action, relations, and state.**

This hybridity is evaluated here as an information-processing capability.

However, the target boundary called “Japanese” also changes historically and over time. The current structure of modern Japanese is not unconditionally projected onto all past and future forms of Japanese.

---

# 8. Kanji and kana

Kanji is not simply “one character, one meaning.” Yet in Japanese use it has a strong ability to separate words and concepts that overlap in sound at the point of written representation.

For example:

```text
意思
意志
医師
```

share a pronunciation but remain distinct semantic slots through writing.

Kana does more than record sound. Particles, inflection, sentence endings, conjunctions, state change, speaker stance, and related information contribute to preserving relational information.

In the comparison model used by this paper, Japanese sentences can, in broad terms:

> **Place semantic/conceptual cores on the kanji side while letting relations, action, and state flow through the kana side.**

This is not a strict one-to-one rule. It is treated as a current structural tendency from the standpoint of Information Engineering.

---

# 9. Context is not necessarily omission

Not all information that is left implicit is missing.

If it is retained in shared context and can be reconstructed when necessary, it is not simple information loss.

In computing terms, it resembles operating on differences while referring to existing state rather than transmitting the entire state every time.

Japanese can omit subjects and objects. If context is not shared, this can cause misrecognition. But when shared context exists, known information need not be repeated, and only new differences can be transmitted.

From an Information Engineering perspective, this can function as compression.

---

# 10. Preserving uncertainty

In information processing, making everything explicit and definite as early as possible is not always optimal.

If unobserved items, multiple interpretations, items not requiring present judgment, or items that may change with future input are fixed early to one value, the system does not gain information. It deletes possibility space.

Japanese is compatible with forms of operation in which some elements such as subject, degree of certainty, stance, or causality remain within context until they need to be fixed.

This paper evaluates that property as:

> **the capacity to preserve uncertainty.**

This evaluation is itself a current judgment dependent on language, use, and observing subject, and is not fixed as a universal one-dimensional performance metric.

---

# 11. Comparison with English

English is an extremely strong operational infrastructure for international standards, APIs, software, technical documents, academic circulation, and international collaboration.

This paper does not reject the use of English.

However:

> **strength in external connectivity**

and

> **ease of preserving semantic structure as the base in which theories and concepts are first generated**

are different evaluation axes.

In the comparison model used here, English centers on linear alphabetic representation and tends to require explicit expansion through lexical choice, word order, modification, and added explanation when fine semantic and relational differences must be preserved.

Japanese can distribute different information across kanji, kana, particles, inflection, omission, context, and related resources.

For the limited purpose considered here, this paper therefore places the role difference:

> **English is strong in external connectivity; Japanese is strong in preserving internal semantic structure.**

This is not an evaluation of the superiority or inferiority of humans, ethnic groups, or cultures. It is a purpose-fit evaluation of base representation from the standpoint of Information Engineering.

If the state of the compared languages, users, LLMs, media, or purpose changes, this comparison is re-audited.

---

# 11.1 Evidence state of comparative claims

Adopting Japanese as the base and normative language of this theoretical system is a **design rule** for the purpose of the paper.

By contrast, claims such as:

- Japanese has higher semantic-structure preservation efficiency than English,
- English is stronger for external connectivity while Japanese is stronger for internal semantic-structure preservation,

are **comparative evaluations that include empirical hypotheses**, separate from the design rule itself.

Therefore, the validity of the base-language rule does not depend on universal empirical proof that Japanese is superior across languages and purposes. Generalizing comparative claims requires separate direct comparisons that fix target documents, users, LLMs, media, purpose, loss function, and reconstructability.

The current Japanese-base rule is maintained, but it is not expanded into the unproven proposition that “Japanese is strongest for every use.”

---

# 12. The “12 colors and 36 colors” analogy

This paper uses the analogy of “12 colors of paint and 36 colors of paint” to explain differences among languages.

It is not a quantitative claim that Japanese has three times as much vocabulary as English.

Even if both systems can create the same final color, a system with fewer initial slots must mix multiple states to create intermediate colors, whereas a system with more initial slots can preserve more intermediate differences as separate states.

The issue is:

> **Not whether a final expression is possible, but how many distinctions can remain separate during information processing.**

This analogy itself is an explanatory Projection, not a quantitative model of language capability.

---

# 13. Cognitive style and language

This paper does not adopt a simple linguistic determinism in which language unidirectionally and completely determines cognition.

As a generative direction, it first places:

```text
cognitive style
↓
required information-processing form
↓
formation / selection of language
```

The differences a human group emphasizes, how it recognizes relations, and what it needs to record are taken to act on language formation.

Once a language is established and inherited, that language in turn acts on the cognitive operations of the next generation.

```text
cognition
↓
language
↓
inheritance
↓
cognition
↓
language
↓
……
```

Cognition and language may therefore recursively reinforce one another.

This causal description is also a current model. If new observations alter the boundary, order, or interaction between cognition and language, the model is reconstructed.

---

# 14. Division of labor among languages in the LLM era

Historically, when the final publication destination was English, there was operational pressure to generate papers and specifications in English from the beginning.

LLMs have greatly reduced the cost of translation, parallel text, style conversion, terminology locking, and auditing translation differences.

As a result, the necessity of making:

> **the language in which a theory is generated**

the same as:

> **the language in which it is published externally**

has decreased.

An original can be established in the language that preserves semantic structure most effectively, and then converted to the required output language afterward.

If this technical condition changes, the rationality of the language division of labor is re-audited.

---

# 15. Japanese-base rule

This theoretical system specifies:

1. **Japanese is the sole base language and normative language.**
2. **The original must always be established in Japanese first.**
3. English and other languages are used only when operationally required for international publication, standards, APIs, applications, collaboration, or similar purposes.
4. Multilingual versions are translations or Projections generated from the Japanese original and are not independent canonical sources.
5. If translation reveals undefined terms, semantic conflicts, missing relations, or insufficient explanation, the translation side does not silently repair them. The Japanese original is re-audited and revised first, after which translation is regenerated.

The operational order is:

```text
cognize and think in Japanese
↓
generate theory in Japanese
↓
define and structure in Japanese
↓
audit in Japanese
↓
establish Japanese original
↓
translate into other languages only when necessary
↓
audit semantic differences against Japanese original
```

This is not merely a translation policy.

> **It is a current specification of the theory-generation process itself.**

The rule is fixed inside the current version. If changed, a new version must state not only that the base language changed but also the effects on theory generation, audit, translation, and the meanings of older originals.

---

# 16. Relation to the Cognitive Engineering system

This paper is not an independent theory of linguistic superiority.

Its position is:

```text
Cognitive Engineering
↓
targeting the world through cognition
↓
establishment of information
↓
Information Engineering
↓
language as infrastructure for information representation and operation
↓
Japanese base
```

This relation itself is a current Projection, not a final hierarchy of the world.

The present Cognitive Engineering system includes **神の領域原理（仮）**, the **Trinity Principle**, and **Closure Phase Ψ**.

The following names also exist:

```text
Human Decision-making System（仮）
人間意思決定理論（仮）
HDS
```

Only the names of HDS are disclosed in this paper.

---

# 17. Time axis and reopening conditions

The Japanese-base rule is a strong current design decision, but it is not permanently immune from revision.

This paper is re-audited from upstream at least if:

- a representational system with higher semantic-structure preservation efficiency than Japanese is established,
- a Japanese-specific cognitive fixation produces major systematic omissions,
- a non-natural-language intermediate representation becomes better suited,
- changes in LLMs, recording media, or translation environments alter the rationality of separating base language from output language,
- the comparison axes “information,” “meaning,” “preservation,” and “efficiency” themselves prove insufficient,
- observations are obtained that change the current relation between cognition and information.

When reopened, past versions are not erased as errors. They remain records under the targets, purposes, and comparison conditions of their time.

---

# 18. Self-application

This paper discusses the ability of language to preserve distinctions.

It therefore audits whether its own current terminology is collapsing distinctions.

For example, broad terms such as:

- “Japanese,”
- “English,”
- “ideographic / phonographic,”
- “semantic structure,”
- “information,”
- “context”

may themselves compress different internal structures into one word.

> **This language theory audits whether it is creating a new Umami Gap of its own.**

---

# 19. Non-goals

This paper does not claim that Japanese people, the Japanese ethnic group, or Japanese culture are superior to others. It does not claim that advanced thought is impossible in English. It does not claim that Japanese always minimizes tokens or maximizes communication speed.

The evaluation target is limited to:

> **Suitability as a base representation for generating, structuring, auditing, and reusing information generated through cognition.**

---

# 20. Conclusion

Information is not an object simply placed in the world.

> **world → cognition → information**

The activities of preserving, transmitting, transforming, computing, retrieving, combining, and reusing information established through cognition are Engineering, not Science.

Therefore, under the current definition of v0.4, this paper does not adopt “Information Science” and treats the relevant activity as **Information Engineering**.

Language is a vast Information Engineering infrastructure through which humanity externalizes, preserves, transmits, and re-inputs information generated through cognition.

Japanese can use on one representational surface: semantic distinctions through kanji, sound/action/relation description through kana, relational information through particles, inflection, and sentence endings, shared-state reference through context, preservation of uncertainty, and simultaneous operation of multiple writing systems and lexical lineages.

That structure is highly suited to the current objective of this theoretical system: semantic-structure preservation efficiency.

Therefore:

> **Japanese is adopted as the base language and normative language.**

This conclusion is operated strongly. At the same time, Japanese, information, cognition, the comparison axes, and the theory-generation environment themselves are not exempted from future re-audit.
